title: Disassembling qLDPC codes for depth-optimal parity-check circuits
authors: Minh T. P. Nguyen, Maximilian Rimbach-Russ, Stefano Bosco
abstract: Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes offer a promising route to scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing, but their practical implementation requires efficient circuits for syndrome extraction. Many qLDPC families are assembled from a small set of components through explicit constructions that imprint edge symmetries on their Tanner graphs. We show that these symmetries can be exploited to design syndrome-extraction circuits from the underlying components, rather than from the full quantum code. For Lifted Product and Balanced Product codes this approach yields an analytical construction with provably optimal or near-optimal CNOT depth. For Quantum Tanner codes it produces depth-optimal circuits on every instance we test, including codes up to nearly 600 data qubits.
summary: This paper presents a novel technique to drastically reduce the circuit depth required for syndrome extraction in qLDPC quantum error-correcting codes. By mathematically 'disassembling' the codes using their inherent symmetries, the authors can solve the scheduling problem on a much simpler graph. This leads to provably optimal or near-optimal CNOT depth circuits for various structured qLDPC families.
main_problem: The primary goal is to design highly efficient, low-CNOT-depth circuits for syndrome extraction in Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check (qLDPC) codes.
main_result: The authors demonstrate a method to achieve depth-optimal or near-optimal CNOT depth for specific qLDPC families (LP and BP codes) by exploiting underlying code symmetries.
method: The core method involves 'disassembling' the complex code structure by quotienting symmetries, solving the scheduling problem on a reduced graph, and then 'lifting' the resulting circuit back to the full code.
model_or_system: The system modeled is the quantum error correction process using qLDPC codes. The circuit structure is analyzed via the Tanner graph, which represents the parity checks acting on data and ancilla qubits.
key_observables: CNOT Depth (the maximum time label $\max 	au(e)$), which must be minimized, and the satisfaction of 'properness constraints' for circuit validity.
important_parameters: The depth bound $\Delta \le \Delta_X + \Delta_Z$, and the structure of the code components (e.g., hypergraph products, group lifts).
main_assumptions: The method assumes that good qLDPC codes possess substantial structure derived from known algebraic operations, and that the properness constraint can be correctly transformed under symmetry partitions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the general process of code assembly/disassembly via symmetry quotienting, the Tanner graph structure for LP codes, and the resulting 'sandwich structure' of the required parity-check circuit schedule (E-M-L bands).
paper_structure: The paper builds from the general problem of syndrome extraction efficiency, details the algebraic framework for exploiting code symmetries (disassembly/reassembly), applies this framework analytically to LP/BP codes, and then applies it numerically to Quantum Tanner (QT) codes.
why_interesting: While focused on quantum computation, the techniques developed—exploiting underlying algebraic symmetries to simplify complex scheduling problems—are highly relevant to optimizing control circuits in any physical quantum system.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Assembling and disassembling codes. A Tan- ner graph T0 is assembled into a qLDPC code TC through a sequence of operations (black arrows). Rather than construct- ing the parity-check circuit directly on TC, we reverse these operations by quotienting the graph edge symmetries (gray arrows), solve the reduced parity-check scheduling problem (edge colors) on T0, and lift the resulting circuit back to TC.

FIG. 2. LP(A, B) codes. (a) Tanner graph TLP, with checks X(i, k) (red), Z(j, l) (green) and data qubits VV(j, k), CC(i, l) (blue). The second line of each vertex is its group coordinate, its position in the fiber over TA □TB. Teal bundles run through [aij]L, [a∗ ij]L and orange bundles through [bkl]R, [b∗ kl]R, one edge per group element of the en- try. (b) Sandwich parity-check circuit for ∆A = ∆B = 4, with P□merging the horizontal edges. Rows give the CNOT layer τ after edge coloring and entries are the color indices. Dashed cells are present only for even degree: ∆A = 3 shortens M by a layer, whereas ∆B = 3 empties one outer entry on each side without narrowing E, L.

FIG. 3. Parity-check circuit of QT codes. Schedule in- duced by the canonical orientation, for C = C′ = [6, 3, 3] of Ref. [36] with ∆= 10. Rows and columns of the base surface are halved (dashed) and given opposite orientations (listed be- side the corresponding half). The four relations compose into a total order in each quadrant, such each schedule per quad- rant has again a sandwich structure; shading marks whether the X- (blue) or Z-families (orange) occupy the middle band.
